newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Dow, Nasdaq seen ripe for correction in 97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Dow, Nasdaq seen ripe for correction in 97.

text.p: U.S. stocks are ripe for a correction in 1997 after a blockbuster year of all-time highs, average forecasts for the Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq Composite indices showed in a Reuters survey of the outlook for the world's top 15 share markets.

But bulls and bears were almost evenly split in the survey's 11 forecasts for each index, the most optimistic predicting the Dow industrials would rise to 7,200 and Nasdaq Composite to 1,600 by the end of next year.
Pessimists saw the Dow as low as 4,500 and Nasdaq at 875 points respectively.

The mean of 11 forecasts contributed for the Dow industrials at end 1997 held out the prospect of a drop over the year to around 6,070 points from around 6,500 on Tuesday. Forecasts from a separate group of 11 analysts saw the technology-rich Nasdaq Composite index at around 1,230 on average in 12 months' time from around 1,310 on Tuesday.

The poll, published on Wednesday, took place during the Dow's first negative week since October. Stocks sank but then recovered last Friday, after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan warned against "irrational exuberance" in stock and other markets.
The Dow reached an all-time high of 6,547.8 on November 25.
Few analysts were able to put numbers to their predictions for 1998, but the three numbers offered for each index all placed them below current levels.
Following is a selection of quotes from analysts who predicted the Dow and Nasdaq levels in this survey:
ALAN NEWMAN, TECHNICAL MARKET ANALYST AT H.D. BROUS & CO

"I think we've overdone it. "We're going into a big corrective phase and it's going to last a long time." Newman said he saw the next two years as a replay of 1973 and 1974 when the stock market did poorly after prices were bid up to overvaluations in the late 1960's and early 1970s.
DAVID SHULMAN, CHIEF EQUITY STRATEGIST AT SALOMON BROTHERS
"Our economists see higher rates so at best we see a sideways market next year or at worst down 10-15 percent. A correction, not a bear market. We had two wonderful years so we may have a pause."
RICKY HARRINGTON, SENIOR VICE-PRESIDENT AND TECHNICAL ANALYST AT INTERSTATE/JOHNSON LANE, CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA

"Earnings are going to disappoint people over the next 12 to 18 months." There had not been a real bear market for 20 years and one was now due at any time. But Harrington predicted recovery in both Dow Jones and Nasdaq Composite in 1998.
ROBERT DICKEY, CHIEF TECHNICAL ANALYST AT DAIN BOSWORTH IN MINNEAPOLIS --

"I think it will be a tough year, down early and staying there for most of 1997." A rise in oil prices would kick off inflation and bring higher interest rates, with the U.S. economy close to or in recession by end of 1997, he said.
JOSEPH BARTHEL, CHIEF INVESTMENT STRATEGIST, FAHNESTOCK & CO --

"I wouldn't be surprised if the market had some weakness going into 1998. If you can look forward, we're in a generational bull market. The focus should be on the big plusses: A ... decline in inflation and interest rates, an ageing population (pouring money into stock mutual funds). I have no reason to suspect we won't see (a Dow) 7600 to 8200."
